_meta.note: hand-curated historic precedents; every claim carries citation_url; consumed by the scenario AI-read as locked facts. Claims without a checkable source were omitted rather than approximated. For the Oxfam 2010 citation, the figures sit in the report PDF downloadable at the cited landing page.

events.name: 2007-08 global food price crisis (rice panic)
events.commodity: rice (with wheat and maize also elevated)
events.trigger: Tight global stocks and high energy prices, then a self-reinforcing cascade of exporter restrictions: Vietnam restricted exports in June 2007, India followed in October 2007, and Pakistan and Thailand joined by May 2008 - four countries representing over 70% of the global rice export market.

price_move.text: The benchmark Thai rice price almost tripled between October 2007 and April 2008.

importers_hit.why: Extreme import dependence and poverty; soaring rice prices triggered deadly riots in April 2008 in which a UN peacekeeper was killed, and the Senate dismissed Prime Minister Jacques-Edouard Alexis on 12 April 2008.

Bread prices rose about 37% between February 2007 and February 2008; around a dozen people died in subsidized-bread queues by March 2008, and a demonstrator was killed in the Mahalla protests of April 2008.

The world's largest rice importer at the time; its state importer NFA had to buy huge volumes into a market where its own traditional supplier Vietnam had largely banned private sales, forcing it into ever-more-expensive tenders.

responses.what: The National Food Authority ran very large, highly public tenders, paying as much as $1,220/t CNF for 25% broken rice - an increase of over $500/t in about a month - and pressed Vietnam publicly for 1.0-1.5 million tonnes of government-to-government supply.
responses.outcome: Backfired: the public mega-tenders and G2G scramble signalled desperation and helped propel world prices higher (Slayton calls the episode 'careless' policy that set the market on fire).

responses.what: President Mubarak ordered the army to take over baking and distribution of subsidized baladi bread; food subsidies were sharply expanded (subsidies for bread, oil, rice and sugar increased, reaching about 2% of GDP in 2008-09).
responses.outcome: Contained the immediate bread-line crisis but at heavy fiscal cost; underlying subsidy-system grievances persisted into later unrest.

responses.what: Egypt banned its own rice exports from April 2008 to keep domestic supply at home.
responses.outcome: Kept some rice at home but added Egypt to the global cascade of export restrictions that was amplifying world prices.

responses.what: India restricted rice exports from October 2007 (Vietnam had begun in June 2007); Pakistan and Thailand joined by May 2008, so that exporters holding over 70% of the market had restricted sales.
responses.outcome: Backfired globally: the export-restriction cascade is identified as the core driver that nearly tripled the benchmark Thai price.

responses.what: In May 2008 Japan announced it would release rice from its WTO-obligation stockpile, offering 300,000 tonnes to the Philippines (50,000 t 'as soon as possible' plus 200,000 t as aid).
responses.outcome: Worked: the announcement alone broke the panic - prices dropped from over $1,100/t to about $800/t by June 2008, before large volumes physically moved.

lessons.text: Export restrictions by dominant suppliers were the main amplifier of the rice spike: once exporters covering over 70% of the market restricted sales, the benchmark price nearly tripled.
A credible announcement of stock release can deflate a panic-driven price bubble: after news that Japan's stockpiled rice would be released, global rice prices fell by 25% in just two weeks.
Political fallout was widespread: some thirty countries saw violent protests over food prices in 2007-08, and in Haiti the crisis brought down the prime minister.
Public panic-buying by a large state importer (Philippines NFA record tenders) fed the very price spiral it was trying to escape.

events.name: 2010 Russian grain export ban
events.commodity: wheat (plus barley, rye, maize and flour)
events.trigger: Severe drought and wildfires in Russia cut wheat production by about 20 million tonnes versus prior seasons, with yields down over 70% in top producing oblasts; Russia banned grain exports effective 15 August 2010, and the ban ran through the 2010/11 season.

price_move.text: Global wheat prices rose 20% in consecutive months (July and August 2010) - per USDA data the only time that happened in the 25 years from 1996 to 2020.

importers_hit.why: World's largest wheat importer, only about 60% self-sufficient and relying on Russia for around half of its wheat imports (44% of 2010 calendar-year imports came from Russia).
Import-dependent for wheat; the government announced a 25% bread price increase citing the world wheat shortage driven partly by Russia's drought and export ban.

responses.what: Ban on exports of wheat, barley, rye, maize and wheat/rye flour, in force from 15 August 2010.
responses.outcome: Stabilized domestic Russian supply but pushed world wheat prices to near two-year highs within days of the announcement.

responses.what: State buyer GASC replaced banned Russian wheat with French and US wheat, paying around $280/t versus roughly $183/t it had been paying for Russian wheat before the ban; former trade minister Rachid Mohamed Rachid put the extra cost to Egypt at $696.8 million in 2010 (figures in the Oxfam report PDF at the cited page).
responses.outcome: Supply was secured but at a large fiscal premium; the episode exposed the cost of single-origin concentration.

responses.what: GASC tender origin mix shifted: in calendar 2010 Egypt imported ~10.5 million tonnes of wheat - 44% Russia, 20% France, 13% US, 7% Ukraine, 5% Australia - with non-Black Sea origins carrying the post-ban months.
responses.outcome: Diversification cushioned the shock; USDA documented Egypt's tender restructuring toward US, French and other origins after August 2010.

responses.what: Government announced bread prices would rise 25% from 6 September 2010 (i.e., passed the shock through rather than absorbing it), alongside water and electricity tariff rises.
responses.outcome: Backfired: riots in Maputo on 1-2 September 2010 left at least 10 people dead and more than 400 wounded as police fired on demonstrators.

lessons.text: A ban by one dominant supplier repriced the whole world market within weeks - wheat rose 20% month-on-month in both July and August 2010, a 25-year record sequence.
Heavy single-origin dependence converts a supplier's domestic policy into an importer's fiscal shock: Egypt's switch to French and US wheat cost it roughly an extra $697 million in 2010.
Passing a supply shock straight into bread prices without compensation triggered deadly unrest in Mozambique within days of the announcement.
The 2010 drought-and-ban episode is widely analyzed as a contributor to the bread-price stress that preceded the 2011 Arab uprisings.

events.name: 2022 Black Sea disruption (Russia-Ukraine war, Grain Initiative and its collapse)
events.trigger: Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine blockaded Black Sea ports; over the preceding three years Russia and Ukraine together accounted for about 30% of global wheat exports and 20% of maize exports.

price_move.text: The FAO Food Price Index hit an all-time record of 159.3 points in March 2022, up 12.6% from February - itself already the highest level since the index began in 1990; world wheat prices alone rose 19.7% during March 2022.

importers_hit.why: World's largest wheat importer; in 2021 it sourced 50% of state and private wheat supplies from Russia and 30% from Ukraine.

Imports nearly 80% of the wheat it consumes, historically almost all from Ukraine (80%) and Russia (16%) as of 2020; the 2020 Beirut port explosion had destroyed the national grain silos, forcing just-in-time imports with minimal storage buffer - all amid a currency and fiscal collapse.

responses.what: GASC cancelled its tenders of 24 and 28 February 2022 after receiving no Black Sea offers and only limited, very expensive French and US Hard Red Winter offers.
responses.outcome: Short-term procurement freeze while the buyer re-planned; demonstrated how fast tender behaviour shifts when a dominant origin goes offline.

responses.what: GASC expanded its approved-origin list to 18 origins (adding India and Kazakhstan among others, alongside the US, EU origins, Argentina, Australia); Egypt received its first private-sector shipment of Indian wheat on 5 June 2022.
responses.outcome: Worked as diversification: Egypt kept bread supply running, though at higher cost, and later resumed heavy Russian buying when Black Sea supply returned.

responses.what: Emergency external financing of wheat imports: parliament approved a $150 million World Bank loan (approved by the Bank in May 2022) to finance wheat purchases and keep Arabic bread affordable; the first 33,000-tonne shipment under the project arrived in February 2023 to rebuild stocks.
responses.outcome: Worked as a bridge: it stabilized bread supply for a country with no reserves, but is a stopgap dependent on external credit rather than a structural fix.

responses.what: India banned wheat exports in mid-May 2022 after a record heatwave (above 50C) slashed harvest prospects, abruptly reversing plans for record shipments that markets had hoped would replace lost Ukrainian supply.
responses.outcome: Backfired globally: CBOT wheat jumped by its 6% daily trading limit and touched an all-time high of $12.68/bu; the G7 criticized the move.

responses.what: Black Sea Grain Initiative (UN/Turkiye-brokered, signed 22 July 2022) created a protected export corridor; almost 33 million tonnes of grain and foodstuffs were exported under it before Russia terminated the deal on 17 July 2023.
responses.outcome: Worked while it lasted: world grain prices eased substantially during the corridor's operation and spiked again on its termination.

lessons.text: Corridor diplomacy is a supply-side fix that demonstrably lowered prices: during the first months of the Black Sea Grain Initiative global wheat prices fell from a peak of $522.29/t in May 2022 to $382.86/t in August 2022.

The corridor's collapse repriced markets immediately: after Russia's July 2023 withdrawal and strikes on Ukrainian grain infrastructure, wheat futures posted their largest one-day rise since February 2022, and the IMF estimated the termination could raise global grain prices by 10-15%.
Knock-on export bans by third countries (India's May 2022 wheat ban, Indonesia's April 2022 palm oil ban) amplified the original shock - the 2008 cascade dynamic repeated.
Importers with no storage buffer (Lebanon after the Beirut silo destruction, importing just-in-time) have days-not-months of resilience and need external financing to bridge shocks.
State buyers adapt tender rules fast: Egypt went from cancelled tenders in late February 2022 to an 18-origin approved list including India and Kazakhstan within months.

events.name: 2023 India rice export restrictions
events.trigger: Domestic rice price inflation and El Nino production concerns: on 20 July 2023 India (about 40% of global rice exports in 2022/23) banned exports of non-basmati white rice with immediate effect; combined with its September 2022 broken-rice ban and export duties, roughly 75-80% of India's rice exports were restricted.

price_move.text: Rice export prices rose to their highest levels in more than a decade after India's restrictions (USDA FAS); global rice prices rose more than 20% following the July 2023 measures as importers scrambled for alternatives (CGIAR).

importers_hit.why: Major broken-rice importer for staple dishes; India supplied as much as 64% of Senegal's total rice imports in 2022 and over 80% in January-August 2023.
The largest global importer of Indian broken rice; Benin, Senegal and Cote d'Ivoire were three of India's top five export markets, each receiving over 1 million tonnes of Indian rice in 2022.

Structural rice importer exposed to world prices; although it buys mainly from Vietnam, global buyers displaced by India's ban shifted demand onto Vietnam and Thailand, sending their export quotes to the highest levels since 2008.
Facing El Nino production shortfalls simultaneously; named by IFPRI among vulnerable countries where rice is 40-67% of caloric intake and import needs were rising.

responses.what: Executive Order No. 39 (signed 31 August 2023, effective 5 September) imposed nationwide retail price caps of P41/kg for regular milled and P45/kg for well-milled rice, citing alleged hoarding and price manipulation on top of the India ban and world prices.
responses.outcome: Backfired/short-lived: retailers took losses and required government subsidies; the caps were lifted in early October 2023 after about a month.

responses.what: Price ceilings were lifted in early October 2023 as supply from the domestic harvest and imports improved.
responses.outcome: Reversal confirmed the cap was a stopgap, not a fix; pressure shifted back to tariff policy and import volumes.

responses.what: Government authorized state logistics agency Bulog to import an additional 2 million tonnes of rice (announced 26 September 2023) to refill reserves and dampen domestic prices amid El Nino shortfalls; total 2023 rice imports reached 3.06 million tonnes, up 613% year-on-year, mostly from Thailand (1.38 Mt) and Vietnam (1.14 Mt).
responses.outcome: Secured supply and market-stabilization stocks, but the surge in demand contributed to record-high Thai and Vietnamese export quotes.

responses.what: After the blanket ban, India carved out government-to-government exemptions, easing the ban for specific partner countries including four African nations (via the National Cooperative Exports Limited channel).
responses.outcome: Partially relieved targeted partners while keeping general market supply restricted; bilateral deals replaced open tenders as the access route.

responses.what: Sub-Saharan importers scrambled for alternative origins as Indian broken-rice exports collapsed 95% year-on-year in August-November 2023 (to 28,500 tonnes).
responses.outcome: Alternatives (Thailand, Vietnam, Pakistan) were found but at world prices more than 20% higher than pre-ban.

responses.what: India lifted the non-basmati white rice export ban in late September 2024 after a strong monsoon and record stocks.
responses.outcome: Global rice prices eased as the dominant exporter returned; the restriction had lasted roughly 14 months.

lessons.text: Concentration risk is extreme in rice: 42 countries source more than 50% of their rice imports from India, and in several African countries India's market share exceeded 80% in 2022 - one exporter's domestic politics became their supply shock.
Retail price caps treated the symptom: the Philippines' caps were abandoned within about a month while world prices stayed high.

Displaced demand cascades to second-tier exporters: buyers shifting from India pushed Thai and Vietnamese quotes to their highest since the 2008 crisis, hurting even importers with no direct India exposure.
Government-to-government exemptions became the main relief valve, favouring states with diplomatic leverage over open-market buyers.

events.name: 2022 Indonesia palm oil export ban
events.commodity: palm oil (crude, RBD, used cooking oil)
events.trigger: Domestic cooking-oil scarcity and price spikes in the world's largest palm oil exporter, amid the global vegetable-oil squeeze from the Ukraine war; export ban imposed 28 April 2022.

price_move.text: The ban ran from 28 April 2022 to 23 May 2022 and was lifted after domestic supply was deemed sufficient and domestic cooking-oil prices declined; the government also set a 10-million-tonne domestic cooking-oil supply safeguard via Domestic Market Obligation rules.

importers_hit.why: India is the world's largest palm oil importer and, with other vegetable-oil importers, faced a market where FAO's vegetable oil price index had already hit record highs in March 2022 due to the Black Sea disruption.

responses.what: Banned exports of crude palm oil, RBD palm oil and used cooking oil from 28 April 2022; revoked the ban effective 23 May 2022 (Ministry of Trade Regulation No. 30 of 2022), citing sufficient domestic supply, declining domestic prices, and the palm sector's importance to large parts of the population.
responses.outcome: Domestic cooking-oil prices declined, but the ban proved unsustainable within four weeks - inventories backed up and the export-dependent producer economy (including smallholders) bore the cost, forcing a rapid reversal.

responses.what: Replaced the ban with Domestic Market Obligation requirements designed to safeguard 10 million tonnes of domestic cooking-oil supply while allowing exports to resume.
responses.outcome: A calibrated domestic-supply carve-out replaced the blunt ban - the compromise most exporters converge on after a ban proves too costly.

lessons.text: Even the dominant exporter of a commodity could not sustain a total export ban for a month: domestic producer losses forced Indonesia to reverse within 25 days and switch to a domestic market obligation instead.
Export bans imposed during an already-tight global market (record FAO vegetable-oil prices in March 2022) stack a policy shock on top of a supply shock for importers.
